turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Right, before you start, his blood pressure just now was 138 over 84, and his pulse was seventy-two, regular.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's helpful. Come and sit yourself down. What brings you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, um, the parking was a nightmare so I'm a bit flustered, but it's the left hand, doctor. It's still a bit weak, and that's really why I've come back.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me how that weakness shows itself day to day.

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I can hold a mug of tea, it's not floppy or anything, but buttons and jar lids are a proper struggle. It's been like that ever since the mild stroke, and that was three months ago. My wife spots it when I'm doing the crossword, she says the pen looks awkward in that hand.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. And how has the walking been?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Walking's alright, honestly. I get to the paper shop and back, maybe a touch slower than before the stroke, but the left leg doesn't drag and it doesn't give way.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about your speech?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Speech is fine now. No slurring, people understand me, even on the phone to the bank which is saying something.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever while this has been going on?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No temperature, I haven't felt hot or shivery at all.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any problems with your chest, cough or getting your breath?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine, no cough, and breathing's normal even on the stairs.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): And your weight, has that shifted?

[SEG0015] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm, I don't really know. The belt's on the same hole I think, though my wife keeps saying the trousers hang looser, and I haven't stood on the scales, so maybe a little, maybe nothing.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's a bit muddy, we'll not chase the scales today. Can I have a look at the hand?
[SEG0017] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, of course. This one.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Grip on the left is a little down compared with the right. The rest of the arm moves well, and your speech sounds clear to me sitting here.
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): That's about what the physio said last month, a slight weakness, nothing dramatic, she was quite pleased actually.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on at the moment?

[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): Aspirin, I was on seventy-five milligrams but no, they changed it, it's a hundred and fifty milligrams once in the morning, by mouth. And atorvastin 40 milligrams at night, and the amlodipine tablet, 5 milligrams once a day, for the blood pressure. I don't miss them, the dosette box sits by the kettle.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good. Anyone in the family with strokes, or sugar, or blood pressure?

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): Err, my father had diabetes in his fifties, type two, on tablets for years until he died. My mother did not, she never had sugar or any of that. And another sister, the one in Leeds, she's got pressure, high blood pressure, but no sugar, she has it checked at her own GP.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): And day to day, how do you fill the week?

[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm still doing the bookkeeping for the little hardware shop on the high street, about 30 hours a week over four mornings. Diet's plain, porridge and a sandwich, not much fried food. I walk the dog most evenings, 20 minutes or so. I have one glass of red wine with supper, and I don't smoke, never have.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): That all sounds very steady. I'd say this is leftover weakness from the mild stroke, not something new starting up.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): So you're not worried it's another one coming?

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): I don't think so, no. We might arrange a scan if the hand does not settle over the next couple of months, but I wouldn't do one today. Keep on with the hand exercises the physio gave you, little and often.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): I will. I do them while the kettle boils, which is often enough, ha.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let's see you back here in three months, and come sooner if the weakness suddenly gets worse or the speech goes off again.
[SEG0031] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book that three-month one at the desk on your way out.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

omissions.text: Left hand weakness affects fine motor tasks: struggles with buttons and jar lids, and pen use looks awkward when doing the crossword.
Patient can still hold a mug of tea; hand is 'not floppy'.
Walking is otherwise alright; patient can get to the paper shop and back.
Negative finding: left leg does not drag.
Negative finding: left leg does not give way.
Negative finding: people understand his speech, including on the phone.
Negative finding: no hot or shivery feelings with the denied fever.
Negative findings from ROS: no chest problems.
Negative findings from ROS: no shortness of breath; breathing normal even on the stairs.
Weight change was asked about and answer was uncertain/equivocal: belt on same hole, trousers may hang looser, has not weighed himself, 'maybe a little, maybe nothing'.
Examination finding: the rest of the left arm moves well.
History: physiotherapist last month also found only slight weakness and was pleased with progress.
Medication adherence: patient says he does not miss his tablets.
Family history negative: mother never had diabetes.
Family history negative: mother never had high blood pressure ('or any of that').
Family history detail: father's type 2 diabetes began in his fifties and was treated with tablets for years.
Family history detail: sister with high blood pressure does not have diabetes.
Doctor reassured patient that he was not worried this was another stroke coming.
